title: Ἶρις ἀπὸ Διός
titleEn: Iris Turns the Goddesses Back — Iliad 8.381–468
about: Hera and Athena arm and drive out of Olympus through the gates that the Hours keep, but Zeus sees them from Ida and sends Iris to stop them. His threat is to lame their horses, throw them from the chariot and leave them wounds that ten years will not heal. Iris meets them at the first gates and delivers the threat, adding a savage word for Athena. Hera gives way and turns the horses; the Hours unyoke them, and the two goddesses sit down among the other gods, grieving. Zeus comes back to Olympus, where Poseidon unyokes his horses, and mocks the pair for their silence and their dread of war. Athena sits sullen and says nothing; Hera cannot hold her anger, and tells Zeus that they know his strength, that they will keep out of the fighting, and that they will only advise the Argives, so that they do not all perish.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, white-armed Hera.
sentences.i: So Athena spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, did not disobey.
sentences.n: Athena’s speech ended at 380, and Hera now does as she asked. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so she spoke’ (ἔφατ’ is the elided imperfect middle of φημί), and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ is a formula for ready obedience; at 5.719 it is said of Athena obeying Hera, and the whole line stands at 5.767, said of Hera obeying Zeus. θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη is ‘the goddess, white-armed Hera’, λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ being her stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἐποιχομένη χρυσάμπυκας ἔντυεν ἵππους
Ἥρη πρέσβα θεὰ θυγάτηρ μεγάλοιο Κρόνοιο·
sentences.l:
She, on the one hand, going to and fro, was making ready the gold-frontleted horses,
Hera, eldest goddess, daughter of great Cronus;
sentences.i: Hera, the eldest goddess, daughter of great Cronus, went about making ready the horses with their golden frontlets;
sentences.n: Hera makes the chariot ready; Athena, who arms herself in the next units, is set against her by αὐτὰρ ‘but’ at 384, and ἣ μὲν ‘she, on the one hand’ looks forward to that. ἐποιχομένη ‘going to and fro’ is the present participle of ἐποίχομαι, and ἔντυεν ‘was making ready’ the imperfect of ἐντύω; the ἐπέντυε of 374 is the same verb with a preverb. χρυσάμπυκας ‘gold-frontleted’ goes with the horses (an ἄμπυξ is a band worn on the brow). The second line names the subject: πρέσβα ‘eldest’ is also a title of honour, θυγάτηρ is ‘daughter’, and Κρόνοιο is the epic genitive in -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
πέπλον μὲν κατέχευεν ἑανὸν πατρὸς ἐπ’ οὔδει
ποικίλον, ὅν ῥ’ αὐτὴ ποιήσατο καὶ κάμε χερσίν,
sentences.i: But Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, let fall on her father’s floor the fine robe, the intricate one, which she herself had made and toiled at with her hands;
sentences.n: The scene turns to Athena. αὐτὰρ ‘but’ marks the turn, and the μέν of πέπλον μὲν is answered by ἣ δὲ ‘and she’ at 387. Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is ‘Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus’ (κούρη ‘girl, daughter’; epic genitive -οιο). κατέχευεν is ‘poured down’, that is, let fall, and πατρὸς ἐπ’ οὔδει is ‘on her father’s floor’. ἑανόν ‘fine’ is uncertain in sense (perhaps ‘soft’ or ‘light’), and ποικίλον ‘intricate’ means worked with a pattern. ὅν ῥ’ is ὅν ῥα ‘which’; ποιήσατο is the aorist middle ‘made for herself’, and κάμε the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’. The unit stops at the comma, because the sentence goes on in the next unit with a new subject.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ χιτῶν’ ἐνδῦσα Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο
τεύχεσιν ἐς πόλεμον θωρήσσετο δακρυόεντα.
sentences.l:
and she, having put on the tunic of cloud-gatherer Zeus,
with arms armed herself for war, tearful.
sentences.i: and she put on the tunic of Zeus who gathers the clouds and armed herself with weapons for tearful war.
sentences.n: Athena arms. ἣ δὲ ‘and she’ answers the πέπλον μέν of 385: she lets the robe fall and puts on a tunic that belongs to Zeus. χιτῶν’ is the elided accusative χιτῶνα ‘tunic’, ἐνδῦσα the aorist participle of ἐνδύω ‘put on’, and Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο ‘of Zeus the cloud-gatherer’ says whose it is (νεφεληγερέτης is a stock epithet, translated every time). τεύχεσιν is the dative plural ‘with arms’, and θωρήσσετο ‘armed herself’ the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω. δακρυόεντα ‘tearful’ agrees with πόλεμον ‘war’, the war that brings tears.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ὄχεα φλόγεα ποσὶ βήσετο, λάζετο δ’ ἔγχος
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν, τῷ δάμνησι στίχας ἀνδρῶν
ἡρώων, τοῖσίν τε κοτέσσεται ὀβριμοπάτρη.
sentences.l:
and onto the chariot, flaming, with her feet she stepped, and took up a spear
heavy, huge, massive, with which she overpowers the ranks of men,
of heroes, with whomever she is angered, she of the mighty father.
sentences.i: She stepped with her feet into the flaming chariot and took up a spear, heavy and huge and massive, with which she beats down the ranks of men, of heroes, with whomever she, the daughter of a mighty father, is angered.
sentences.n: She mounts the chariot and takes her spear. ἐς … βήσετο is ‘stepped into’, an epic mixed aorist without augment, and the plural ὄχεα stands for one chariot; φλόγεα ‘flaming’ is from φλόξ ‘flame’, and the poet does not say whether it shines or burns. The first line (389) is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of φλόγεα, short by nature, has to be counted long, as the long syllable that opens the third foot. λάζετο is ‘took hold of’. The last two lines describe the spear in the words of the Odyssey (1.100–101), and the English is the Odyssey’s: δάμνησι ‘she overpowers’ (epic ending -ησι), στίχας ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων ‘the ranks of men, of heroes’, τοῖσίν τε κοτέσσεται ‘with whomever she is angered’. ὀβριμοπάτρη ‘she of the mighty father’ is an epithet of Athena alone.

sentences.t: Ἥρη δὲ μάστιγι θοῶς ἐπεμαίετ’ ἄρ’ ἵππους·
sentences.l: And Hera swiftly with the whip reached out at the horses;
sentences.i: And Hera quickly laid the whip to the horses;
sentences.n: Hera now drives. μάστιγι is the instrumental dative ‘with the whip’, and θοῶς ‘swiftly’ the adverb of θοός. ἐπεμαίετ’ is the elided imperfect middle of ἐπιμαίομαι ‘reach at, touch’, which with a whip means laying it on; ἄρ’ is the particle ἄρα ‘then’.

sentences.t: αὐτόμαται δὲ πύλαι μύκον οὐρανοῦ ἃς ἔχον Ὧραι,
sentences.l: And of themselves the gates of heaven bellowed, which the Hours kept,
sentences.i: Then of their own accord the gates of heaven, which the Hours kept, bellowed;
sentences.n: The gates of heaven open for the chariot. αὐτόμαται ‘of themselves’ is the nominative plural feminine, agreeing with πύλαι ‘gates’, and οὐρανοῦ is the genitive ‘of heaven’. μύκον ‘bellowed’ is a past tense without augment of μυκάομαι ‘low, bellow’, the sound that cattle make. ἃς ἔχον Ὧραι is ‘which the Hours kept’: the Ὧραι ‘Hours’ are goddesses who guard the gates.

sentences.t:
τῇς ἐπιτέτραπται μέγας οὐρανὸς Οὔλυμπός τε
ἠμὲν ἀνακλῖναι πυκινὸν νέφος ἠδ’ ἐπιθεῖναι.
sentences.l:
to whom are entrusted great heaven and Olympus,
both to open and to shut the solid cloud.
sentences.i: Great heaven and Olympus are in their charge, both to open and to shut the solid cloud.
sentences.n: The charge of the Hours. τῇς is the epic dative plural feminine of the relative, ‘to whom’, and ἐπιτέτραπται the perfect passive of ἐπιτρέπω ‘entrust’, with μέγας οὐρανὸς Οὔλυμπός τε ‘great heaven and Olympus’ as the things entrusted. ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’. ἀνακλῖναι ‘to lay back’ and ἐπιθεῖναι ‘to put on’ are aorist infinitives; because the cloud works like a door, the English gives their sense, ‘to open’ and ‘to shut’. πυκινόν is ‘solid’.

sentences.t: τῇ ῥα δι’ αὐτάων κεντρηνεκέας ἔχον ἵππους.
sentences.l: That way, through them, the goad-driven horses they drove;
sentences.i: Through these gates they drove their goad-driven horses;
sentences.n: The two goddesses drive out. τῇ ‘that way’ and δι’ αὐτάων ‘through them’ refer to the gates; αὐτάων is the epic genitive plural feminine of αὐτός. ἔχον is ‘drove’, and its plural shows that both goddesses are in the car. κεντρηνεκέας is built on κέντρον ‘goad’ and a root meaning ‘carry’, and is usually taken to mean ‘driven on by the goad’; the exact sense is not known.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ Ἴδηθεν ἐπεὶ ἴδε χώσατ’ ἄρ’ αἰνῶς,
Ἶριν δ’ ὄτρυνε χρυσόπτερον ἀγγελέουσαν·
sentences.l:
And Zeus the father, from Ida, when he saw, was incensed dreadfully,
and Iris he urged on, gold-winged, to tell the news;
sentences.i: When father Zeus saw them from Ida, he was dreadfully incensed, and he urged gold-winged Iris on to bring news:
sentences.n: Zeus has been on Ida since 8.47, and he sees the goddesses set out. Ἴδηθεν is ‘from Ida’ (-θεν marks the place from which). ἐπεὶ ἴδε is ‘when he saw’, ἴδε being the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (= εἶδε); the Greek gives it no object, and ‘them’ is supplied. χώσατ’ is the elided χώσατο, the aorist middle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, and αἰνῶς is ‘dreadfully’. ὄτρυνε is an unaugmented past tense of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. χρυσόπτερον ‘gold-winged’ is made from χρυσός ‘gold’ and πτερόν ‘wing’, and ἀγγελέουσαν is the future participle of ἀγγέλλω, in its uncontracted epic form (Attic ἀγγελοῦσαν), giving the purpose: ‘to bring news’.

sentences.t:
βάσκ’ ἴθι Ἶρι ταχεῖα, πάλιν τρέπε μηδ’ ἔα ἄντην
ἔρχεσθ’· οὐ γὰρ καλὰ συνοισόμεθα πτόλεμον δέ.
sentences.l:
“Go, set out, Iris swift, turn them back, and do not allow them face to face
to come; for not fairly shall we come together, to war.
sentences.i: “Be off with you, swift Iris, and turn them back; do not let them come face to face with me, for it will not go well if we meet in war.
sentences.n: Zeus’s order to Iris. βάσκ’ ἴθι ‘go, set out’ is the pair that sent Dream at 2.8: βάσκε is the imperative of βάσκω, a lengthened form related to βαίνω, and ἴθι the imperative of εἶμι. Ἶρι ταχεῖα is a vocative, ‘swift Iris’ (ταχεῖα is the feminine of ταχύς). πάλιν τρέπε is ‘turn back’, an imperative; μηδ’ ἔα is ‘and do not allow’, the imperative of ἐάω, with the infinitive ἔρχεσθ’ (ἔρχεσθαι) ‘to come’. The Greek names neither the two goddesses nor the person they must not face; both are understood, and ἄντην is ‘face to face’. In οὐ γὰρ καλά, καλά is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘fairly, well’; συνοισόμεθα, the future middle of συμφέρω, is ‘we shall come together’, which with πτόλεμον δέ ‘to war’ (the epic form of πόλεμον, with -δε of direction) means to clash in battle.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: For thus I will declare, and this too fulfilled shall be;
sentences.i: For I will say it in this way, and what I say will also be fulfilled:
sentences.n: Zeus now says what he will do. The line is word for word the one in which Athena promises Achilles gifts at 1.212, and its English is kept. ὧδε is ‘in this way’; ἐξερέω is ‘I will say out’, ἐκ with the future of εἶπον. τετελεσμένον is the perfect passive participle of τελέω, ‘fulfilled’, and ἔσται ‘will be’. What follows is what will be fulfilled.

sentences.t:
γυιώσω μέν σφωϊν ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους,
αὐτὰς δ’ ἐκ δίφρου βαλέω κατά θ’ ἅρματα ἄξω·
sentences.l:
I will lame, for you two, under the chariot, the swift horses,
and yourselves out of the chariot I will throw, and break the chariot to pieces;
sentences.i: I will lame the swift horses of you two as they draw the chariot, throw you yourselves out of the chariot, and break it to pieces;
sentences.n: Zeus names the penalty. γυιώσω is the future of γυιόω, from γυῖα ‘limbs’ (the word is in 452): to take the strength out of the limbs, here of the horses, so ‘lame’. σφωϊν is the dual dative, ‘for you two’, which with ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ‘under the chariot’ (the horses stand yoked beneath it) says whose horses are meant; ἅρμασιν is a plural for one chariot, as ὄχεα was at 389. αὐτάς ‘yourselves’ is the feminine accusative plural, standing for the pair. ἐκ δίφρου βαλέω is ‘I will throw out of the chariot’, βαλέω being the uncontracted future of βάλλω. κατά … ἄξω is a tmesis, for κατάξω, ‘I will break to pieces’, the future of κατάγνυμι.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἐς δεκάτους περιτελλομένους ἐνιαυτοὺς
ἕλκε’ ἀπαλθήσεσθον, ἅ κεν μάρπτῃσι κεραυνός·
sentences.l:
Nor even until the tenth years, as the years come round,
will you two be healed of the wounds which the thunderbolt may seize;
sentences.i: and not even when the years have come round to the tenth will you two be healed of the wounds that the thunderbolt may lay on you;
sentences.n: The lasting harm. οὐδέ κεν … ἀπαλθήσεσθον is ‘nor will you two be healed’, a future dual (second person) of ἀπαλθήσκομαι ‘be healed of’ (related to ἀλθαίνω ‘heal’), with κεν; ἕλκε’ is the elided ἕλκεα ‘wounds’, the accusative saying what is healed. ἐς δεκάτους περιτελλομένους ἐνιαυτούς is ‘until the tenth years, as they come round’: δεκάτους ‘tenth’ is an ordinal, περιτελλομένους the present participle middle of περιτέλλομαι ‘come round’, and ἐνιαυτούς are ‘years’. In ἅ κεν μάρπτῃσι κεραυνός, ἅ is the relative ‘which’ (the wounds), μάρπτῃσι the subjunctive of μάρπτω ‘seize’ (epic ending -ῃσι), and κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’ the subject.

sentences.t: ὄφρα ἰδῇ γλαυκῶπις ὅτ’ ἂν ᾧ πατρὶ μάχηται.
sentences.l: so that she may see, the gleaming-eyed one, whenever she fights with her own father.
sentences.i: so that the gleaming-eyed goddess may see, whenever she fights with her own father.
sentences.n: The threat ends on Athena. ὄφρα ἰδῇ is a purpose clause, ‘so that she may see’, the aorist subjunctive of ὁράω; the Greek gives it no object. γλαυκῶπις stands alone, ‘the gleaming-eyed one’, a stock epithet used as a name for Athena (the old explanation is ‘owl-eyed’; the sense is not certain). ὅτ’ ἂν … μάχηται is ‘whenever she fights’, with the subjunctive, and ᾧ πατρί ‘her own father’ has the possessive ὅς, not the relative.

sentences.t: Ἥρῃ δ’ οὔ τι τόσον νεμεσίζομαι οὐδὲ χολοῦμαι·
sentences.l: At Hera not so much do I feel resentment, nor am I filled with anger;
sentences.i: I do not feel so much resentment at Hera, nor am I filled with anger;
sentences.n: Zeus sets Hera aside. Ἥρῃ is the dative of the person at whom the feeling is directed, with νεμεσίζομαι ‘I feel resentment’ (the same verb as in Hera’s own speech to him at 5.757). τόσον is ‘so much’, and οὔ τι τόσον ‘not so very much’. χολοῦμαι is the present middle of χολόω ‘be filled with anger’, from χόλος ‘anger’, so that the line says ‘resentment’ and ‘anger’ in turn; οὐδέ joins the two verbs.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γάρ μοι ἔωθεν ἐνικλᾶν ὅττί κεν εἴπω.
sentences.l: for always to me she is accustomed to thwart whatever I may say.”
sentences.i: for it is always her habit to thwart me, whatever I say.”
sentences.n: Zeus gives the reason: Hera always opposes him, so her defiance is nothing new. ἔωθεν is the third singular of the perfect ἔωθα ‘be accustomed’, with movable ν, and the Greek gives it no subject; Hera is understood. μοι is the dative ‘me’, the person thwarted. ἐνικλᾶν is an infinitive of ἐνικλάω, built on κλάω ‘break’; it is usually taken to mean ‘cross, thwart’, but the exact sense is not certain. ὅττί κεν εἴπω is ‘whatever I may say’, the aorist subjunctive with κεν, and ὅττι is the old form of ὅ τι. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δὲ Ἶρις ἀελλόπος ἀγγελέουσα,
βῆ δ’ ἐξ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἐς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose up Iris, storm-footed, to tell the news,
and went from the Idaean mountains to tall Olympus.
sentences.i: So Zeus spoke, and storm-footed Iris set out to bring news; she went from the mountains of Ida to tall Olympus.
sentences.n: Iris sets out. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’, and ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose up, started’. Ἶρις ἀελλόπος ἀγγελέουσα is the subject: ἀελλόπος ‘storm-footed’ is taken from ἄελλα ‘storm’ and πούς ‘foot’ (the second part is not quite certain), and the participle ἀγγελέουσα, ‘to bring news’, is the same one as at 398, now in the nominative. ἐξ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων is ‘from the Idaean mountains’, and μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον, ‘tall Olympus’, is the house rendering of the stock phrase.

sentences.t:
πρώτῃσιν δὲ πύλῃσι πολυπτύχου Οὐλύμποιο
ἀντομένη κατέρυκε, Διὸς δέ σφ’ ἔννεπε μῦθον·
sentences.l:
And at the first gates of many-folded Olympus
meeting them, she held them back, and of Zeus to them she told the word:
sentences.i: At the first gates of many-folded Olympus she met them and held them back, and told them the word of Zeus:
sentences.n: Iris stops the goddesses at the gates of Olympus, which are probably the gates of heaven that opened at 393, though the poet does not say so. πρώτῃσιν … πύλῃσι is ‘at the first gates’, the epic dative plural in -ῃσι. πολυπτύχου ‘of many folds’ (πολύς ‘many’ and πτυχ- ‘fold’) names the folds and hollows of the mountain’s flanks. ἀντομένη is the participle of ἀντάω ‘meet’, and κατέρυκε ‘held back’ the past tense of κατερύκω. σφ’ is the elided σφε ‘them’, and ἔννεπε ‘told’ takes it as well as μῦθον ‘word’, so Διὸς … μῦθον is ‘the word of Zeus’.

sentences.t: πῇ μέματον; τί σφῶϊν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μαίνεται ἦτορ;
sentences.l: “Where are you two set on going? Why in the wits of you two is the heart raging?
sentences.i: “Where are you two set on going? Why is the heart raging in your minds?
sentences.n: Iris’s speech opens with two questions. μέματον is the second person dual of μέμονα, a perfect with present sense, ‘be eager, be set on’, with a verb of going understood. σφῶϊν is the dual dative ‘of you two’, here the possessive sense, and ἐνὶ φρεσί ‘in the wits’ has ἐνί for ἐν. μαίνεται ἦτορ is ‘the heart is raging’, μαίνεται the present middle of μαίνομαι. The edition ends both questions with the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἐάᾳ Κρονίδης ἐπαμυνέμεν Ἀργείοισιν.
sentences.l: He does not allow it, the son of Cronus, to come to the defence of the Argives.
sentences.i: The son of Cronus does not allow you to come to the defence of the Argives.
sentences.n: The reason Iris gives. ἐάᾳ is the present of ἐάω ‘allow’ in its open epic form (Attic ἐᾷ), and the Greek gives it no object; ‘you’ is supplied from the questions. Κρονίδης is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus. ἐπαμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive in -έμεν (= ἐπαμύνειν) of ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence of’, with the dative Ἀργείοισιν ‘the Argives’; the poet’s choice among the three names of the army is kept in the English.

sentences.t:
ὧδε γὰρ ἠπείλησε Κρόνου πάϊς, ᾗ τελέει περ,
γυιώσειν μὲν σφῶϊν ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους,
αὐτὰς δ’ ἐκ δίφρου βαλέειν κατά θ’ ἅρματα ἄξειν·
sentences.i: For this is what the son of Cronus has threatened, and he will carry it out: to lame the swift horses of you two as they draw the chariot, to throw you yourselves out of the chariot, and to break it to pieces;
sentences.n: Iris passes Zeus’s threat on in indirect speech, so the verbs of 402–403 become infinitives: γυιώσειν and ἄξειν are future infinitives and βαλέειν an aorist infinitive (the uncontracted form of βαλεῖν); the words are those of the earlier lines. ἠπείλησε is ‘threatened’, and Κρόνου πάϊς is ‘the son of Cronus’ (πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς). ᾗ τελέει περ is not certain: ᾗ may be the adverb ‘in the way that’, or the editors’ ἦ ‘truly’ may lie behind it, and τελέει is the uncontracted future of τελέω ‘fulfil’; either way the sense is that he will carry the threat out.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἐς δεκάτους περιτελλομένους ἐνιαυτοὺς
ἕλκε’ ἀπαλθήσεσθον, ἅ κεν μάρπτῃσι κεραυνός·
sentences.l:
Nor even until the tenth years, as the years come round,
will you two be healed of the wounds which the thunderbolt may seize;
sentences.i: and not even when the years have come round to the tenth will you two be healed of the wounds that the thunderbolt may lay on you;
sentences.n: Iris repeats 404–405 word for word, and the English is the same; the grammar is explained there. She speaks as a messenger, giving Zeus’s words as he gave them.

sentences.t: ὄφρα ἰδῇς γλαυκῶπι ὅτ’ ἂν σῷ πατρὶ μάχηαι.
sentences.l: so that you may see, gleaming-eyed one, whenever you fight with your father.
sentences.i: so that you, gleaming-eyed one, may see, whenever you fight with your father.
sentences.n: Where Zeus spoke of Athena in the third person (406), Iris speaks to her. γλαυκῶπι is the vocative of γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed one’, ἰδῇς the aorist subjunctive of ὁράω ‘you may see’ (without an object, as before), and μάχηαι the present subjunctive middle in its open epic form (Attic μάχῃ). σῷ πατρί is ‘your father’; σός is the ordinary possessive ‘your’, not the possessive ὅς of 406.

sentences.t:
Ἥρῃ δ’ οὔ τι τόσον νεμεσίζεται οὐδὲ χολοῦται·
αἰεὶ γάρ οἱ ἔωθεν ἐνικλᾶν ὅττι κεν εἴπῃ·
sentences.l:
At Hera not so much does he feel resentment, nor is he filled with anger;
for always to him she is accustomed to thwart whatever he may say;
sentences.i: He does not feel so much resentment at Hera, nor is he filled with anger; it is always her habit to thwart him, whatever he says;
sentences.n: Iris gives Zeus’s words about Hera in the third person. νεμεσίζεται and χολοῦται are the third singular of the verbs Zeus used in the first person at 407, and οἱ is the weak dative ‘to him’ (Zeus), where Zeus said μοι ‘to me’. The rest is as at 408: ἔωθεν ‘she is accustomed’, ἐνικλᾶν ‘to thwart’ (sense not quite certain), and ὅττι κεν εἴπῃ ‘whatever he may say’, the subjunctive in the third person.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ αἰνοτάτη κύον ἀδεὲς εἰ ἐτεόν γε
τολμήσεις Διὸς ἄντα πελώριον ἔγχος ἀεῖραι.
sentences.l:
But you, at least, most dread dog, fearless one, if truly
you will dare against Zeus a huge spear to lift.”
sentences.i: But you, most dreadful dog, you fearless one — if you truly dare to lift your huge spear against Zeus.”
sentences.n: Iris turns on Athena with an insult, and the sentence breaks off with no outcome stated: the threat already given is the outcome. κύον is the vocative of κύων ‘dog’, here said to a goddess, with αἰνοτάτη ‘most dread’ (the superlative of αἰνός) in the feminine to agree. ἀδεές, from ἀδεής, is ‘without fear’; it may be a second vocative, ‘fearless one’, or an adverb (‘fearlessly’), and the English takes the first. εἰ ἐτεόν γε τολμήσεις is ‘if truly you will dare’, ἐτεόν being ‘truly’ and τολμήσεις a future. Διὸς ἄντα is ‘against Zeus’, face to face, and ἀεῖραι is the aorist infinitive of ἀείρω ‘lift’ (Attic ἄραι), with πελώριον ἔγχος ‘huge spear’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις,
αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίην Ἥρη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken went away, swift-in-feet Iris,
but Athena Hera addressed with a word:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Iris, swift of foot, went away; and Hera spoke to Athena:
sentences.n: Iris leaves, and Hera speaks. ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη is a formula for a departure after a speech (‘she, then, so having spoken, went away’); ἣ μὲν is answered by αὐτάρ ‘but’ in the next line, and πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις, ‘Iris, swift of foot’, is her stock epithet; πόδας is an accusative of respect, ‘in the feet’. Ἀθηναίην Ἥρη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘Hera addressed Athena with a word’: πρὸς … ἔειπεν is a tmesis, and ἔειπεν the aorist of εἶπον with its doubled ε.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος, οὐκέτ’ ἔγωγε
νῶϊ ἐῶ Διὸς ἄντα βροτῶν ἕνεκα πτολεμίζειν·
sentences.l:
“Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, no longer I, for my part,
the two of us allow, against Zeus, for the sake of mortals, to fight;
sentences.i: “Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, I no longer allow the two of us to fight against Zeus for the sake of mortals;
sentences.n: Hera gives way. ὢ πόποι is an exclamation, ‘ah’, and αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος is ‘child of aegis-bearing Zeus’, Athena (αἰγιόχοιο is the epic genitive in -οιο). οὐκέτ’ ἔγωγε is ‘no longer I, for my part’; νῶϊ is the dual accusative ‘the two of us’, and ἐῶ the present of ἐάω ‘allow’, which takes the infinitive πτολεμίζειν (the epic form of πολεμίζειν ‘fight’). Διὸς ἄντα is ‘against Zeus’, and βροτῶν ἕνεκα ‘for the sake of mortals’, with ἕνεκα following its noun.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἄλλος μὲν ἀποφθίσθω, ἄλλος δὲ βιώτω,
ὅς κε τύχῃ· κεῖνος δὲ τὰ ἃ φρονέων ἐνὶ θυμῷ
Τρωσί τε καὶ Δαναοῖσι δικαζέτω, ὡς ἐπιεικές.
sentences.l:
Of these let one perish, and let another live,
whoever may chance; and let that one, his own things thinking in his heart,
for the Trojans and the Danaans give judgement, as is fitting.”
sentences.i: Let one of them perish and another live, whichever it may chance to be; and let Zeus, thinking his own thoughts in his heart, give judgement between the Trojans and the Danaans, as is fitting.”
sentences.n: Hera leaves the mortals to Zeus. τῶν ‘of these’ points to the mortals, and ἄλλος μέν … ἄλλος δέ is ‘one … another’; ἀποφθίσθω and βιώτω are third singular imperatives (ἀποφθίσθω is the aorist middle of ἀποφθίνω ‘perish’, βιώτω the aorist of βιόω ‘live’). ὅς κε τύχῃ is ‘whoever may chance’, the aorist subjunctive of τυγχάνω with κε and no object stated, so ‘as it may fall’. κεῖνος ‘that one’ is Zeus, who is not named in this sentence (he is in 427–428). τὰ ἃ is the possessive ὅς, neuter plural, ‘his own things’, not the relative, and φρονέων ἐνὶ θυμῷ is ‘thinking in his heart’. δικαζέτω is the present imperative of δικάζω ‘give judgement’, with the datives Τρωσί … Δαναοῖσι; ὡς ἐπιεικές is ‘as is fitting’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα πάλιν τρέπε μώνυχας ἵππους·
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, back she turned the solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and turned the solid-hoofed horses back;
sentences.n: Hera turns the chariot. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα is ‘so then, having spoken’ (an aorist participle, feminine). πάλιν τρέπε is ‘she turned back’: at 399 the same two words were Zeus’s command to Iris, and there τρέπε was an imperative, but here it is an unaugmented past tense, so the English differs. μώνυχας ἵππους is the stock phrase ‘solid-hoofed horses’ (μώνυξ ‘with an undivided hoof’).

sentences.t:
τῇσιν δ’ Ὧραι μὲν λῦσαν καλλίτριχας ἵππους,
καὶ τοὺς μὲν κατέδησαν ἐπ’ ἀμβροσίῃσι κάπῃσιν,
ἅρματα δ’ ἔκλιναν πρὸς ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα·
sentences.i: The Hours loosed the fair-maned horses for them, tethered them at the ambrosial mangers, and leaned the chariot against the gleaming inner wall;
sentences.n: The Hours, who kept the gates, now serve the goddesses. τῇσιν is the epic dative plural feminine of the pronoun, ‘for them’, and λῦσαν the aorist of λύω with the epic ending -αν (Attic ἔλυσαν). καλλίτριχας ‘fair-maned’ agrees with ἵππους, and καὶ τοὺς μέν is ‘and these’, the article as a pronoun. κατέδησαν is ‘tethered’, from καταδέω. κάπῃσιν are ‘mangers’, and ἀμβροσίῃσι ‘ambrosial’ says the horses of the gods are fed on ambrosia. ἅρματα is a plural for one chariot, and ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα is ‘the shining inner wall’, παμφανόωντα being an uncontracted participle of παμφαίνω ‘shine all over’. Lines 434–435 echo the Odyssey (4.39–42), and the English of 435 is the Odyssey’s, without ‘of the porch’, which the Odyssey’s i adds.

sentences.t:
αὐταὶ δὲ χρυσέοισιν ἐπὶ κλισμοῖσι κάθιζον
μίγδ’ ἄλλοισι θεοῖσι, φίλον τετιημέναι ἦτορ.
sentences.l:
and they themselves on golden seats sat down
mingled with the other gods, grieved in their dear heart.
sentences.i: and they themselves sat down on golden seats among the other gods, grieving in their hearts.
sentences.n: The two goddesses take their places. αὐταί ‘they themselves’ sets them against the horses and the chariot, and κάθιζον is the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’. κλισμοῖσι is the dative plural of κλισμός ‘seat’, the house word, with χρυσέοισιν ‘golden’ (epic -έοισιν). μίγδ’ is the elided μίγδα ‘mingled with’, with the dative ἄλλοισι θεοῖσι. τετιημέναι is the feminine plural perfect participle of the verb whose dual Zeus uses at 447, ‘be troubled’; φίλον … ἦτορ is an accusative of respect, ‘in their dear heart’.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ Ἴδηθεν ἐΰτροχον ἅρμα καὶ ἵππους
Οὔλυμπον δὲ δίωκε, θεῶν δ’ ἐξίκετο θώκους.
sentences.l:
And Zeus the father, from Ida, the well-rolling chariot and horses
to Olympus drove, and came to the council-seats of the gods.
sentences.i: Father Zeus drove his well-rolling chariot and horses from Ida to Olympus, and came to the gods’ seats of council.
sentences.n: Zeus comes back. The opening words Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ Ἴδηθεν are those of 397. ἐΰτροχον ‘well-rolling’ is built on ἐΰ ‘well’ and τροχός ‘wheel’ (the diaeresis is as the edition prints it). Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’, with -δε of direction, and δίωκε ‘drove’ is an unaugmented imperfect of διώκω, which usually means ‘pursue’ but here is said of driving a chariot. ἐξίκετο is ‘came to’, the aorist middle of ἐξικνέομαι, and θώκους are ‘council-seats’ (θῶκος ‘seat’), here the seats where the gods sit.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ καὶ ἵππους μὲν λῦσε κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος,
ἅρματα δ’ ἂμ βωμοῖσι τίθει κατὰ λῖτα πετάσσας·
sentences.l:
And for him also the horses loosed the famous earth-shaker,
and the chariot upon the pedestals he set, spreading a linen cloth over it;
sentences.i: The famous earth-shaker loosed the horses for him as well, and set the chariot on its pedestals, spreading a linen cloth over it;
sentences.n: Poseidon serves Zeus as the Hours served the goddesses, but the Greek does not name him: κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος is ‘the famous earth-shaker’, a stock phrase. τῷ is ‘for him’, the article as a pronoun, and λῦσε the aorist of λύω. ἂμ βωμοῖσι is ἀνὰ βωμοῖσι ‘upon the pedestals’ (ν becomes μ before β); a βωμός is a raised base, and the word is more often used of altars, but no sacrifice is in view here. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι ‘set’, and ἅρματα is again a plural for one chariot. κατὰ … πετάσσας is a tmesis, ‘spreading over’, the aorist participle of πετάννυμι with the doubled σ of verse, and λῖτα is ‘linen cloth’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δὲ χρύσειον ἐπὶ θρόνον εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἕζετο, τῷ δ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶ μέγας πελεμίζετ’ Ὄλυμπος.
sentences.l:
And he himself, on a golden chair, far-thundering Zeus,
sat down, and under his feet great Olympus was shaken.
sentences.i: Zeus who thunders from afar took his seat himself upon a golden chair, and great Olympus shook beneath his feet.
sentences.n: Zeus sits. χρύσειον is the epic form of χρυσοῦν ‘golden’, and θρόνον is ‘chair’, the house word. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is a stock phrase: the second part of εὐρύοπα (‘voice’ or ‘eye’) is disputed, and the house rendering keeps the traditional ‘far-thundering’. ἕζετο is the aorist middle of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’. πελεμίζετ’ is the elided imperfect passive πελεμίζετο, from πελεμίζω ‘shake’, and τῷ … ὑπὸ ποσσί is ‘under his feet’, with the epic dative plural ποσσί.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ οἶαι Διὸς ἀμφὶς Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη
ἥσθην, οὐδέ τί μιν προσεφώνεον οὐδ’ ἐρέοντο·
sentences.l:
And those two, alone, apart from Zeus, Athena and Hera,
sat, and not a word to him did they speak, nor ask him anything;
sentences.i: But Athena and Hera sat by themselves, apart from Zeus, and did not say a word to him or ask him anything;
sentences.n: The two goddesses say nothing. αἳ δ’ ‘and those two’ is the article as a pronoun, and οἶαι ‘alone’ the feminine plural nominative; Διὸς ἀμφίς is ‘apart from Zeus’. ἥσθην is the dual of ἧμαι ‘sit’. προσεφώνεον ‘spoke to’ and ἐρέοντο ‘asked’ (the epic form of ἔρομαι) are plural verbs with a dual subject, and the rest of the line is as at 1.332. μιν is the enclitic ‘him’, Zeus.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: But he knew in his own wits, and spoke:
sentences.i: But he understood in his own mind, and spoke:
sentences.n: Zeus notices their silence. αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘but he’, Zeus. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘know, recognise’, and the Greek gives it no object; the speech that follows shows that he has read their silence. ᾗσιν is the possessive ‘his own’ (= ἑῇσιν), not a relative, and φρεσί ‘in the wits’ the dative plural of φρήν with ἐνί for ἐν. φώνησεν is ‘lifted his voice, spoke’. The line is the same as 1.333, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: τίφθ’ οὕτω τετίησθον Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη;
sentences.l: “Why so are you two grieved, Athena and Hera?
sentences.i: “Why are you two so grieved, Athena and Hera?
sentences.n: Zeus’s mocking question. τίφθ’ is ‘why’, a by-form of τίπτε (τί and ποτέ), and τετίησθον the dual of the perfect middle of the verb whose participle, τετιημέναι, stands at 437: ‘be grieved, troubled’. Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη is the subject, the pair named as one.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν θην κάμετόν γε μάχῃ ἔνι κυδιανείρῃ
ὀλλῦσαι Τρῶας, τοῖσιν κότον αἰνὸν ἔθεσθε.
sentences.l:
Surely you have not grown weary, I suppose, in the man-glorifying battle,
destroying the Trojans, against whom a fearsome resentment you have set up.
sentences.i: Surely you two have not grown tired of destroying the Trojans in the battle that brings men glory, the Trojans against whom you have taken up a fearsome resentment.
sentences.n: Zeus’s irony. οὐ μέν θην is ‘surely not, I suppose’, and κάμετον is the dual aorist of κάμνω ‘grow weary’, with the participle ὀλλῦσαι ‘destroying’ (feminine, from ὄλλυμι) agreeing with the two goddesses. μάχῃ ἔνι is ‘in battle’, with ἔνι placed after its noun, and κυδιανείρῃ ‘man-glorifying’ is the dative of the stock epithet. τοῖσιν is ‘against whom’, referring to the Trojans, and κότον αἰνὸν ἔθεσθε is ‘you have set up a fearsome resentment’: ἔθεσθε is the aorist middle of τίθημι, a plural verb with a dual subject. κότος is lasting resentment, kept apart from χόλος ‘anger’.

sentences.t:
πάντως, οἷον ἐμόν γε μένος καὶ χεῖρες ἄαπτοι,
οὐκ ἄν με τρέψειαν ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ.
sentences.l:
In any case, such as my might is, and my hands, invincible,
not would they turn me back, as many gods as are on Olympus.
sentences.i: In any case, such is my might and such are my invincible hands that all the gods there are on Olympus could not turn me back.
sentences.n: Zeus boasts. πάντως is ‘in any case’, and οἷον is ‘such as’, so that οἷον ἐμόν γε μένος καὶ χεῖρες ἄαπτοι reads ‘such is my might and such are my hands’. ἄαπτοι is of uncertain sense and origin; it is usually glossed ‘invincible’ (as if ‘not to be laid hold of’), and the translation keeps that. οὐκ ἄν με τρέψειαν is ‘they could not turn me back’, the aorist optative with ἄν, and ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ ‘as many gods as are on Olympus’ is its subject.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊν δὲ πρίν περ τρόμος ἔλλαβε φαίδιμα γυῖα
πρὶν πόλεμόν τε ἰδεῖν πολέμοιό τε μέρμερα ἔργα.
sentences.l:
But you two, even before, trembling took hold of your glorious limbs,
before war to see, and of war the baneful deeds.
sentences.i: But trembling took hold of your glorious limbs even before you saw war and the baneful deeds of war.
sentences.n: He turns the taunt on their courage. σφῶϊν is the dual dative ‘of you two’, a possessive with γυῖα ‘limbs’, and πρίν περ is ‘even before’. τρόμος ἔλλαβε ‘trembling took hold of’ has ἔλλαβε as an augmented aorist of λαμβάνω, with the doubled λ of verse. φαίδιμα ‘glorious’ is the house word for φαίδιμος. πρὶν … ἰδεῖν is ‘before seeing’, πρίν with the infinitive. μέρμερα is of uncertain origin, usually taken as ‘baneful’, said of the works of war.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δέ κεν τετελεσμένον ἦεν·
sentences.l: For thus I will declare, and this would have been fulfilled;
sentences.i: For I will say it in this way, and it would have been fulfilled:
sentences.n: Zeus begins as at 401, with the same words ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, but here the second half has κεν and the imperfect ἦεν (the epic form of ἦν): ‘and it would have been fulfilled’, what would have happened if the two had gone on. τὸ is ‘this’, the article as a pronoun, and τετελεσμένον the perfect passive participle of τελέω.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἐφ’ ὑμετέρων ὀχέων πληγέντε κεραυνῷ
ἂψ ἐς Ὄλυμπον ἵκεσθον, ἵν’ ἀθανάτων ἕδος ἐστίν.
sentences.l:
Not in your chariot, struck by the thunderbolt,
back to Olympus would you two have come, where the seat of the immortals is.”
sentences.i: Struck by the thunderbolt, you two would not have come back in your chariot to Olympus, where the seat of the immortals is.”
sentences.n: What Zeus would have done. οὐκ ἂν … ἵκεσθον is ‘you two would not have come’, ἂν with a dual past form of ἱκνέομαι (the form is ambiguous and could also be read as a short-vowel subjunctive, but the context asks for the past sense). ἐφ’ ὑμετέρων ὀχέων is ‘in your chariot’ (ὑμέτερος ‘your’, plural; the plural ὀχέων stands for one chariot), and πληγέντε is the dual aorist passive participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, with κεραυνῷ ‘by the thunderbolt’ as a dative of means. ἂψ is ‘back’, and ἵν’ is ‘where’. ἀθανάτων ἕδος ἐστίν is ‘the seat of the immortals is’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἳ δ’ ἐπέμυξαν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη·
πλησίαι αἵ γ’ ἥσθην, κακὰ δὲ Τρώεσσι μεδέσθην.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they muttered, Athena and Hera;
close together those two sat, and evils for the Trojans they were contriving.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Athena and Hera muttered; they sat close together, contriving evils for the Trojans.
sentences.n: Zeus has finished, and the two goddesses answer with sounds, not words. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ = ἔφατο), and αἳ δ’ ‘and they’ turns to the pair. ἐπέμυξαν is an aorist of ἐπιμύζω ‘mutter’, a low sound made with the lips closed; the same two lines stand at 4.20. πλησίαι is feminine plural ‘near’, ἥσθην the dual of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and μεδέσθην the dual of μέδομαι ‘plan’, with κακά ‘evils’ as its object, so that the two sit close together planning harm for the Trojans.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι Ἀθηναίη ἀκέων ἦν οὐδέ τι εἶπε
σκυζομένη Διὶ πατρί, χόλος δέ μιν ἄγριος ᾕρει·
sentences.l:
Athena indeed was in silence and said nothing at all,
being sullen at father Zeus, and savage anger had hold of her;
sentences.i: Athena for her part stayed silent and said nothing at all, sullen toward her father Zeus, and savage anger took hold of her;
sentences.n: Athena and Hera now part ways. ἤτοι (one word in the edition) sets Athena against Hera in 461. ἀκέων ἦν ‘was in silence’ and οὐδέ τι εἶπε ‘and said nothing at all’ make the same point twice. σκυζομένη is the participle of σκύζομαι ‘be sullen’, with Διὶ πατρί ‘at father Zeus’. χόλος ‘anger’ is the subject of ᾕρει, the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘seize’ with its augment, and μιν is ‘her’. The two lines stand at 4.22–23 too.

sentences.t: Ἥρῃ δ’ οὐκ ἔχαδε στῆθος χόλον, ἀλλὰ προσηύδα·
sentences.l: But Hera’s breast did not hold the anger, but she spoke out:
sentences.i: But Hera’s breast could not hold her anger, and she spoke out:
sentences.n: Hera cannot keep silent. Ἥρῃ is a dative of possession, ‘Hera’s’, and στῆθος ‘breast’ the subject of ἔχαδε, the aorist of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’. The ἀλλά ‘but’ sets her against Athena’s silence in the line before. προσηύδα ‘she spoke out’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω, with no object stated; the speech that follows is addressed to Zeus. The line is the same as 4.24.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: Hera’s first words are a rebuke. αἰνότατε is the vocative of αἰνότατος, the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, and Κρονίδη is ‘son of Cronus’, addressed to Zeus. ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ‘what sort of word’ carries the article, which gives the sense ‘this word’, and ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with its doubled ε. The edition ends this line with a full stop although it is a question.

sentences.t: εὖ νυ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν ὅ τοι σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν·
sentences.l: well indeed we too know that your strength is not feeble;
sentences.i: we too know very well that your strength is not feeble;
sentences.n: Hera repeats Athena’s words to Zeus at 8.32, with one change. εὖ νυ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν is ‘well indeed we too know’, ἴδμεν being ἴσμεν, from οἶδα. ὅ τοι σθένος is ‘that your strength’ (ὅ is the conjunction, τοι = σοι), and οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν ‘not feeble’ puts ἀλαπαδνός where Athena’s line has ἐπιεικτόν ‘yielding’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης Δαναῶν ὀλοφυρόμεθ’ αἰχμητάων,
οἵ κεν δὴ κακὸν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες ὄλωνται.
sentences.l:
but all the same we grieve for the Danaan spearmen,
who indeed, having filled up an evil fate, shall perish.
sentences.i: but all the same we grieve for the Danaan spearmen, who will fill up an evil fate and perish.
sentences.n: She turns to the army. ἔμπης is ‘all the same’; ὀλοφυρόμεθ’ is the first plural of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament, grieve for’, with the object in the genitive Δαναῶν … αἰχμητάων (epic -άων for -ῶν), ‘the Danaan spearmen’. In the relative clause, οἵ κεν δὴ … ὄλωνται is ‘who, indeed, shall perish’, ὄλωνται being the aorist subjunctive of ὄλλυμι with κε; κακὸν οἶτον ἀναπλήσαντες is ‘having filled up an evil fate’, οἶτος ‘fate, doom’, the aorist participle of ἀναπίμπλημι ‘fill up’. The two lines are the same as Athena’s at 8.33–34, and the English is kept.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι πολέμου μὲν ἀφεξόμεθ’, εἰ σὺ κελεύεις·
sentences.l: But indeed from war we will hold off, if you bid;
sentences.i: But we will indeed keep away from the war, if you so bid;
sentences.n: Hera gives way, as Athena did at 8.35, but with a condition. ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but indeed’ (ἤτοι is one word as the edition prints it); ἀφεξόμεθ’ is the future middle of ἀπέχω with its vowel cut off, ‘we will hold ourselves off from’, with the genitive πολέμου ‘war’. εἰ σὺ κελεύεις is ‘if you bid’, where Athena’s line has ὡς σὺ κελεύεις ‘as you bid’.

sentences.t: βουλὴν δ’ Ἀργείοις ὑποθησόμεθ’ ἥ τις ὀνήσει,
sentences.l: but a plan to the Argives we will suggest, such as will profit,
sentences.i: but we will suggest to the Argives a plan that will do them good,
sentences.n: What she offers instead. βουλὴν δ’ Ἀργείοις ὑποθησόμεθ’ is ‘but a plan to the Argives we will suggest’, ὑποθησόμεθα being the future middle of ὑποτίθημι ‘suggest, advise’ with its vowel cut off. ἥ τις ὀνήσει is ‘such as will profit’: ἥ is the relative ‘which’, τις ‘any’, and ὀνήσει the future of ὀνίνημι ‘profit, do good to’. The line is the same as 8.36, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: ὡς μὴ πάντες ὄλωνται ὀδυσσαμένοιο τεοῖο.
sentences.l: so that not all may perish, you being angry.”
sentences.i: so that they may not all perish while you are angry.”
sentences.n: The purpose of her plan. ὡς μὴ … ὄλωνται is ‘so that not … may perish’, a negative purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive. ὀδυσσαμένοιο … τεοῖο is a genitive absolute, ‘you having been angry’: ὀδυσσάμενος is the aorist participle of ὀδύσσομαι ‘be angry’, and τεοῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘of you’. The line is the same as 8.37, and Hera’s speech ends here.
